speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTIONS FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with respect to this notice of motion. The point of order I wish to raise is to the effect that in the light of the privileges and practices of the house this matter should not be dealt with in the way proposed, and further that consideration should be given to the form of this motion before we reach the point at which it is moved for debate. I do not 29180-231
contend that it is necessary for Your Honour to rule on my point of order today, but in view of the fact that this is the first opportunity for me to raise the point of order I felt I should do so at this moment lest I be out of court if I left it until later.
Standing order 50 reads as follows:
Whenever Mr. Speaker is of the opinion that a motion offered to the house is contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament, he shall advise the house thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon, and quote the standing order or authority applicable to the case.
I do not contend that there is a precise rule or standing order governing this matter. Indeed, there are no standing orders that tell us how to revise our standing orders. I do contend, however, that dealing with the matter in this way is contrary to the privileges of parliament, and I make that contention on three grounds. In the first place I draw the attention of Your Honour and the house to the fact that on other occasions when the rules of the House of Commons have been subjected to a thorough overhaul, it has been done by referring the matter to the committee of the whole house. I contend, therefore, that it is against the privileges of parliament to ask us to deal with this major overhaul with the Speaker in the chair, which gives us no opportunity to deal with the various rules one by one.
May I take a moment to document my contention that the privileges of parliament are clear so far as our past practice is concerned. In 1867, the first time there was any revision of the rules this parliament inherited from the parliament of the former Province of Canada, a motion was made on December 28 to refer the proposals made by the committee at that time to the committee of the whole house.
The next time the rules were revised was in 1876, and the same practice was followed. If you will consult Hansard for that year, at page 905, for March 29, 1876, you will find that the matter was referred to the committee of the whole house. The rules were dealt with seriatim by that committee of the whole house, and subsequently the house gave them both second and third reading.
December 9, 1968

Proposed Changes in Procedure [DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
In other words, it was clear in the early days that these were matters that had to be dealt with as being of substance and importance; that the house had to have an opportunity to deal with the rules individually in committee as well as to pass on them in the house itself.
The next major overhaul came in 1906. Again, if one refers to Hansard of July 9 of that year, page 7459, he will find that Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved the motion to refer to the committee of the whole house the report of a special committee on procedure which had been presented earlier. The same thing happened in 1910 when there was another major overhaul. The motion was made on April 29 of that year, as recorded at page 8336 of Hansard. Again it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who made the motion to refer the committee's report to the committee of the whole house.
The next occasion when there was a major change in the rules of the house was in 1913.
I will come back to it later, rather than dealing with it at this point, because it presents a very interesting exception to the rule. After that the next occasion was 1927. On March 18 of that year, as recorded in Hansard at page 1337, Mr. Lapointe moved that the report of the committee that had been tabled be referred to the committee of the whole house.
The next occasion was 1944. On March 7 of that year Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King moved that the committee's report which had been tabled be referred to the committee of the whole house. That was the first occasion upon which I participated in a debate on procedure. I remember it very well. It did not get very far; certain members were against it, it bogged down in committee of the whole, and that committee's report was never adopted.
The next occasion was 1955, when we had a very thorough study under the direction of Hon. Walter Harris. The report of the committee was presented and on June 14, as recorded in Hansard at page 4751, Mr. Harris moved that the matter be dealt with in the committee of the whole house, and this was done commencing July 1 of that year. The next major overhaul came in 1965. On that occasion Mr. Pearson on June 8, as recorded in Hansard at page 2129, moved that the matter be dealt with in the committee of the whole house.
So our practice over the years is clear. Changing our rules is not something we do by


a sudden death motion with Mr. Speaker in the chair, which gives us no opportunity to deal with the rules seriatim. It has almost always been done by referring committee reports to the committee of the whole house.
There are some exceptions to this practice, and I draw attention to them quite frankly. These exceptions do not alter the general rule. For example, there have been a number of occasions when committee reports proposed temporary changes. I had the privilege of moving some of them myself. They were moved with Mr. Speaker in the chair. There were a few occasions when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) was prime minister, when the same thing was done when some temporary rules were put in for one year, then another year and continued. There was no objection to its being done that way, so it was done on that occasion by adopting a report with Mr. Speaker in the chair.
I submit that in all these instances there was general consent to its being done in that way and they do not invalidate the established practice that whenever there is a major overhaul the committee's report is referred to the committee of the whole house.
The only exception to this rule so far as any substantial change is concerned was in the year 1913. I hope my hon. friends to the right will not take umbrage if I again express some criticism of the Tories of that day. The Tories of today are a little different; they are now Progressive Conservatives.

speechtext:
On
that occasion back in 1913, Sir Robert Borden was prime minister. As all students of history know, parliament was engaged in the naval aid bill debate, which went on and on and on. In due course the government of the day stopped the debate right in the middle of it and brought in a motion to amend the rules. One of the changes proposed in that motion was the introduction of the infamous closure rule, which we now have as standing order 33. The matter was not referred to a committee of the whole house; it was done on a government motion with Mr. Speaker in the chair. But I hope no Liberal will cite that precedent. If he should, I would ask him to read the oratory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who then sat on the opposition side of the house and condemned the whole practice out of hand. One of the things Sir Wilfrid Laurier complained about was the very fact that the
December 9, 1968	COMMONS
matter was not being dealt with in committee of the whole house. I submit that the position taken by the Liberal leader of that day still holds at the present time.
So that is my first point. The others will not take so long. My first point is that the privileges of the house are clear, the rules are ours, and we have the right to be protected against one motion covering a whole host of rules, some of which we are for and some of which we are against. This denies us the opportunity to consider carefully this important matter. As I said, it has been done every time, except once, by reference to committee of the whole house, and that one time is not a precedent because it was opposed bitterly by the Liberals of the day. Furthermore, even on that occasion it was not a case of a report from a special committee but was rather a straight government motion on the order paper.
The second point I wish to make is that I have found at least one case-there may be others-where concurrence in a report with Mr. Speaker in the chair did not put into effect what was contained in the report. I will not take the time of the house to go into this now-I will be glad to present a memorandum on the point-but I submit there was some doubt as to whether the mere concurrence in a report with Mr. Speaker in the chair without the rules having been considered seriatim in committee of the whole would effect changes in our standing orders.
The third point is that I contend that although this motion seems proper because there is provision in the rules for motions to concur in committee reports, it is a disguised way of making us deal with a complicated question on one vote. May I remind Your Honour that on June 15, 1964, Mr. Speaker Macnaughton had to deal with this issue on the occasion of the flag debate, and those who were here will remember that that motion in its first form contained two separate sections. Some of us contended it was a complicated matter and we had the right to have it divided into its constituent parts. There was a procedural argument about it and Mr. Speaker Macnaughton gave his ruling on the day I indicated. That ruling is to be found in Hansard from page 4303 to page 4306. Mr. Speaker Macnaughton went over our own practices; he also went over the practices of the British House of Commons, and in the end he relied on standing order 1 of our rules which says that if nothing is provided for in our rules we have to go by the practices in the British house.

The precedents in the ruling he gave on that occasion made it clear that it is the Speaker's duty to see to it that members are not put in the position where they have to vote at once on several phases of a matter, to some of which they may be opposed and others which they may be prepared to support. I submit that this is what we are being presented with in disguise in the fourth report which is mentioned in the motion on the order paper at the moment, which contains some proposals which I for one am quite happy to support. It also contains at least one proposal to which I am strongly and bitterly opposed. I contend that I personally have the right to vote separately on those different rules in committee of the whole, and I contend that parliament as a whole has this right.
I found some interesting quotations in my research into these experiences during the past hundred years. One of them which amused me was back in 1876 when the rules were being revised. The house went into committee of the whole in the proper way. But one member complained bitterly that the changes in the rules were not going far enough. In fact he said, "If we don't watch out the sessions are going to get longer; they will be three months a year instead of two." This was in 1876. I also found many occasions when the chairman of the special committee, usually the Speaker himself, said to the house that the way we must deal with this is not on a partisan basis, not on the basis of government versus opposition, but in the full recognition that these are the rules of the parliament of Canada, a parliament that belongs not to us but to all the people. I submit, therefore, that we should not be confronted with any short cuts. We should deal with these rules in a way that has been made clear by the practices of this House of Commons for the past 100 years.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
I can just deal briefly, Mr. Speaker, with the three points brought up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. His first proposition was that it is one of the privileges of the house that the rules should be amended by a procedure whereby a resolution is put in the committee of the whole house. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the precedents cited by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indicated that there are at least two procedures for dealing with
December 9, 1968

Proposed Changes in Procedure changes in the rules of the house. These changes can be dealt with either by way of a resolution to be dealt with in committee of the whole, as indicated in certain examples by the hon. member, or alternatively in the manner of proposals made in a committee and the recommendation that the report of the committee should be considered with Mr. Speaker in the chair. This procedure has equal validity.
I suggest there were really these two options open and we have chosen the one option, namely that of dealing with these very complicated matters through a report of the special committee on procedure and a motion for concurrence in that report. I point out that in recent years, on April 26, 1967, an order of the house was adopted covering some fairly complicated changes in the rules. As the hon. member says, those changes were made on a provisional basis; neverthless they were complicated, and this was done by concurrence in a committee report. This was the case, too, with regard to a permanent change which was made in the rules by concurrence in a committee report recommending a time limit for the ringing of the bells.
There are, therefore, precedents to support both these vehicles for getting house approval of these particular measures. I would therefore disagree with the argument advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he says there is only a unique procedure for doing this when you have complicated and perhaps controversial proposals.
I should like to make reference to one other matter which the hon. member mentioned, and that is that this is a complicated question and therefore is not to be decided on one single vote. I point out in the first place that the house decided, and I think it was a wise decision, that changes of the scope which have been considered in the special committee on procedure are perhaps better made by a small representative group of members in a special committee on procedure rather than in the house as a whole. I would say that is so because it was found necessary to hold no less than 26 sessions of that particular committee, and to invoke the assistance of the people at the table as well as other officers of the house for the purpose of drawing up these very complicated changes in the standing orders. I make the basic argument, therefore, that if changes are to be made, those changes should be made in a special committee on procedure because that is the most effective forum for dealing with such an examination.


It is acknowledged at once there is not general support for all the proposals. It is really because of this non-support of the whole of the report of the special committee on procedure that there was not a single report but three reports. The first report was merely for the purpose of explaining the attitude of the committee toward the proposals, and a general description of the changes. The second report contains the principal changes in the standing orders and also those which are the most subject to controversy. The third report on the order paper, the fifth report of the committee, incorporates those changes, which it has been assumed by the special committee on procedure will not be of a controversial nature and will probably find general acceptance in the house.
It is not true to say that the hon. member who has just spoken or any other hon. member will be without a vehicle for expressing his disagreement with what the committee has done, or without a vehicle for getting any committee decision changed. I suggest, given the complicated nature of the subject matter and given the complicated nature of the discussions which have taken place, probably the most appropriate manner for having the proposals changed is by taking the action that is open to hon. members, namely by moving an amendment to refer the report back to the special committee on procedure so the committee might further consider the report along certain lines, which would be suggested in the amendment to the original motion for concurrence in the report.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the two principal points made by the hon. member are, if I may express the last one first, that the house would not have an opportunity to express its opinion on the various proposals; and in answer I contend this opportunity does exist under the present procedure. The first of his two points is that there is a compelling precedent that requires rule changes of this kind to be dealt with in only one way; and I contend this argument is wrong, and wrong in face of the very precedents cited by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which indicate that either procedure has been and is acceptable to the house in changing the standing orders of the house.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: USE OF DRYING FACILITIES AT LAKEHEAD ELEVATORS
speechtext:
In the
absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatchewan, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the question of grain drying at the lakehead terminals been resolved on a 24-hour, seven day basis, or is drying still being carried out on a six day basis?

maintopic: USE OF DRYING FACILITIES AT LAKEHEAD ELEVATORS
speechtext: I have the impression that this matter has been discussed at some length in the house, but I will gladly refer it to the ministers involved.

maintopic: USE OF DRYING FACILITIES AT LAKEHEAD ELEVATORS
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, on November 27 Your Honour, in disallowing a motion that this entire subject be debated, ruled that the wheat situation was a continuing emergency. This being so, the other day I asked that the Prime Minister should have at least one minister available to answer questions concerning this problem, for every day on which plant is idle at the lakehead, 260,000 bushels are left undried. Mr. Speaker, we have now lost one and a half months, during which something like 25 million bushels could have been dried at the lakehead.
This question has still not been resolved, and I have no opportunity to ask the ministers directly concerned what is being done about it. Moreover, neither the Minister of Transport nor the Minister without Portfolio, who answers questions in connection with the transport of wheat, is available for questioning. I believe it to be my duty to raise questions on this pressing matter on any opportunity which presents itself. I am sure the Prime Minister can revise the roster and see that one responsible minister is here so that hon. members may receive a reply more satisfactory than an undertaking to refer the questions raised to the appropriate minister provided he is available. Mr. Speaker, he should be available on all occasions, because this problem has been with us for a long time. I suggest I have every right to stand up each day in the house and ask questions which I believe to be extremely pressing and important.

I do want, however, to take advantage of this opportunity to make a brief statement covering certain important points in connection with Devco.
A great number of subjects relating to the operations of the corporation were raised before the standing committee, and, I hope, satisfactorily answered. There is, however, one point of such importance that I feel it should be restated to the house as a whole.
The main objective of the corporation, as is well known, is to rationalize the coal mining operations but to do so only in a way compatible with the social obligations that we have to the miners. There has been, with good reason, a great deal of concern among the people' of Cape Breton and the members of the standing committee about the possible hardship and dislocation which may be caused in the lives of employees. I can assure hon. members that the corporation recognizes its very fundamental social obligations. I can further assure members that the government will be watching closely to ensure that these obligations are fulfilled.
The first step in the corporation's program will be to introduce and implement the proposed pre-retirement leave plan. Until the corporation knows how many employees are going to take advantage of that plan, it is difficult to be specific about the details or the timetable for future operations. Accordingly, the plan is sufficiently flexible to ensure that coal mining operations will be adjusted to the labour force situation, so that no miner has to be discharged before he is entitled to preretirement leave unless there is a job for him to go to.
The corporation will be opening the new Lingan mine. That will in itself provide new work while the mine is being developed as well as after it is in production. In addition, the corporation is busily seeking to attract other industrial developments on the island of Cape Breton. The pace at which operations in the existing mines are reduced will depend on the pace at which, for these reasons, alternative jobs become available for the miners.
This is the essence of the plan. I invite members to consider whether any painful industrial situation of this kind, where an industry has to suffer a major contraction, has ever before been dealt with by methods as farsighted and humane.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must be a very naive member and a very uninformed former union leader because I would normally have expected a report such as this, coming before the house-independently of political parties because it is not exclusively the work of the people on this side, but a joint effort with the Nova Scotia government and labour unions-to stir up at least a little enthusiasm and satisfaction with what a corporation, which I do not own personally but which belongs to all Canadians, has managed to do, something extremely difficult, while safeguarding the fundamental interests of the workers.
I confess that I am disappointed, not because there is criticism-that is normal, even what seems perfect can always be criticized-but because there is a lack of enthusiasm, a lack of gratitude towards those who worked. I do not mean the government but those who really try to help the miners and help the development of Cape Breton, Not only is there is no enthusiasm, but there is even an attempt to minimize the efforts that were made, and I shall explain it.
The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis) spoke of a $2,400 pension for bachelors with no dependents, and of a $3,000 pension for those with dependents. There is more than that, Mr. Chairman. A bonus of $50 for each year of service up to a maximum of $500 is given to those who are forced to retire and they receive a comparable sum when they reach 65, which is the normal retirement age.
The provisions in the act concerning the leave prior to receiving the pension also provide for the payment of a certain percentage to compensate for the 2 per cent increase in the cost of living.
Mr. Chairman, I have spent my whole life negotiating collective agreements and trying to protect the workers. I have known a great

DEBATES	December 9, 1968
many affiliated unions both in the C.L.C., the old C.I.O. and the central which I represented. I have seen all sorts of agreements concluded in similar circumstances. Not a single one of them, Mr. Chairman, remotely resembled this one or could be compared to it, whatever the strength of the unions represented. The Canadian government, in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia, the miners and their representatives, seems to understand the problem rather better than some of the hon. gentlemen in this house.
All these people, in my opinion, are creating an extremely interesting precedent. I have not seen anything like it, Mr. Chairman, not even when I had to deal with other industrial concerns, for example the shipyards in Lau-zon. The hon. member for Frontenac has left, but he could perhaps have compared the two cases earlier. The George T. C. Davie company decided to close down because it is not making enough money. Workers are dismissed without any pension or any protection whatsoever. Nevertheless, they are Canadian citizens like you and me, as the coal miners of Cape Breton. They are human being who have responsibilities, who enjoy life; but they have received nothing at all. They will have to get unemployment insurance and if they cannot find a job, they will be distitute. That is one case among others.
It is not because I regret what is happening in Cape Breton Mr. Chairman, because I do not regret it. I feel that what is going on in Cape Breton should happen everywhere in Canada. We should not allow people to be harmed as they are very often when plants are shut down. They are merely left with their small pension or they have to obtain unemployment insurance, because they have no other choice. Here are workers who remain with an uneconomic business which costs the Canadian government $28 million a year. Every ton of coal extracted costs the government and the company $15 and brings $6. It takes a long time to make money that way.
This is a truly unprofitable undertaking and if it had been administered by private individuals-that is to say, if the government had not taken an interest in it, and here I am talking about the Nova Scotia government as well as the federal government, it was not a matter of pettiness-they would have laid off those people years ago. They would have closed the coal mines and, in fact, those people would be in the most dire need.
December 9, 1968

But under an agreement, the Devco-of course that is its task and, no matter how it is interpreted, reading the preamble to the act is enough to be convinced-was set up to put an end to the production of coal in Nova Scotia unless it becomes profitable. That is the very objective of the undertaking and it is clearly stated in the Act.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
It is very well to refer to past speeches or statements, but the legislation which was passed by the Canadian parliament, is very clear. But according to the legislation, workers must be taken care of and given human working conditions, and Devco does that.
The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond wonders by what right-and he appeals to my trade union experience-an employee can be forced to retire at 60, or be encouraged to retire between 50 and 55?
Unfortunately, there is in our society no legal right to a function. Under what statute do I breathe? I do not know. Under what statute is an employee without work dismissed? None that I am aware of. No worker, except in very special cases, has a legal right to the job he holds. That is why, every day, employers lay off workers who are no longer needed, and the unemployment insurance or other social welfare programs take those workers in charge.
I do not need to find a statute that authorizes Devco to do the same. Furthermore, the hon. member could read section 18 of the Act, which provides for the retirement of coal miners. I do not have to refer to other statutes. If that were the only problem to solve, it could be done easily. It is clear that Devco has not only the right to do such a thing but, according to the law, everything shows that it has the obligation to retire miners who are no longer needed, but also to make sure at the same time that those people are treated in a human way.
The honourable member suggests that I be more generous with regard to the pensions. I could be, it is not my money. However, I feel that for 150 reasons-for which I am not responsible-the workers of Cape Breton are really, at the present time and compared to the rest of the Canadian workers, getting very special treatment, which I would personally like to see generalized and incorporated in our statutes.
I do not mean that the Cape Breton miners are exploiting the Canadian society. That is not true. That is not what I mean. What I
Supply-Regional Development mean is simply that they are fortunate in having, at the present time, the government of Canada as an employer; and that does not mean that the government members are the only ones who take into account and protect the interests of those people.
Obviously, that money comes from the Canadian taxpayers. Perhaps $10,000 a year, $15,000 or more could be given those miners. But, keeping in mind the average salary and what is now going on in our Canadian society, I feel that the coal miners in Cape Breton are not ill-treated. On the contrary, they are getting better treatment than any of the workers I have ever known, and surely I have known as many as most of those now sitting in this house.
Naturally, they will not go to Florida with $3,000 a year, plus two $500 bonuses and a 2 per cent increase in their annual income. They will certainly not buy yachts on that kind of an income. But there are many Canadians wo do not go to Florida, who do not own yachts and who do not have a $3,000 annual pension, that is normal in that field. The member is shocked and says that the miner in fact is paying the Canadian government or Devco a subsidy. Let us not carry absurdity too far. The whole undertaking now exists thanks to government subsidies. It could not survive a single day were it not for the money of the Canadian government. So, to say that the miners pay a subsidy to Devco is really, to my mind, overstepping the mark.
Mr. Chairman, as far as coal is concerned, I believe the house has good reasons to be happy; those who are responsible for the setting up of Devco have made a very good job of it. I hope the Devco's authorities will soon come to an agreement with the Miners' Union so that the collective agreement will be signed and, thus the purposes of the legislation achieved.
The case of the railwaymen has been mentioned earlier. I think that the point raised is important and serious. The solution will not be easy to find, and I do not intend to discuss it here, in the house, this afternoon. However, I am prepared to admit that a particular problem exists there and I shall no doubt have the opportunity of discussing the matter with the people involved in order to try to find a solution to this problem. Apart from that, I think that the Devco plan corresponds exactly to the letter and spirit of the legislation passed by the House of Commons.

Mr. Chairman, if I may express a wish, I would like some day all workers in Canada to enjoy the same kind of protection in the same circumstances. If the labour unions ever succeeded in reaching that goal, I think they could congratulate themselves.
As to development, at this time one can talk indefinitely about it. The member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) seems surprised that after eight months no definite development plan has been brought forward. Perhaps he knows more than we do on the subject, but at all events I would have been surprised if there had been one.
When I think of ARDA in the lower St. Lawrence, when I consider what is happening now on Prince Edward Island, and what happened to all the programs established not only by us but also by all provincial governments, I suggest that after eight months, it would be unfair to cast stones at Devco and blame it for not having found magical solutions to the development problems Cape Breton Island.
Certainly some elements for solution, have been found and efforts are being made, but I think it is too early to either applaud or to criticize.
Personally I think that Devco should be congratulated. The opening of the Lingan is considered by some to-day as a mere trifle, but for me and for the miners I have met, it is more than a trifle, it is truly a harbinger of hope, and that is what counts for them; I believe that the miners must be happy, even if some people here, in the house, see the dark side of everything-as dark as coal. In my opinion, Devco has done its work well.
On the other hand, I think it is too early to judge. However, I am well aware that construction of a motel has been discussed. Obviously, Devco does not intend to develop the tourist industry as it would be unwise in the first place and rather childish. However, if some economic development is to be achieved in Cape Breton Island and if technicians are to be attracted there, there are housing problems to consider. It will be necessary for Devco to accommodate these people in Sydney if they are invited and are interested. This is quite a secondary aspect and it has no bearing on development as such. This is indirectly connected and it is somewhat premature, I think, to blame Devco at this point.
I was asked why Dosco was making money at the present time, since it was taken over 
by the government, while as a private enterprise, it was losing money. There are several reasons, and not just one, as some would seem to think.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I do think that this example would not be enough to prove that any government corporation is necessarily more efficient than private enterprise, precisely because Dosco assets were obtained at a very good price. In fact, what we will pay for Dosco will certainly be a terrific bargain which does not happen every day. Capital costs are much lower and besides, at the present time, there is a good morale among Dosco workers which did not exist previously. It seems that a new cooperation prevails and even that the present unity of management is also one of the reasons why the company now makes a profit. There is also the market, since the railway track market is rather prosperous at present and Dosco benefits therefrom.
I do not think one can come to any conclusion, but if one wants to know why Dosco is now economically sound, whereas it was not before, I think it is not enough to say simply that the state took over, although I am not ready to speak favourably at this point of the efficiency of the managers of Dosco before the state took over.
Anyhow, the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked me whether an agreement had been reached with Dosco and with the companies which had businesses before. I know that negotiations are taking place. Unfortunately, I do not know what stage has been reached, and I can give no information on the subject at this time. I know that lawyers are meeting and that discussions are taking place, but I am completely in the dark as to their results.
Mr. Chairman, this is a most interesting experience from a human point of view. I am referring to Dosco and Devco. This experience shows that the interests of the workers can very well be looked after. The government of Canada and those who dealt with the situation on behalf of the government of Nova Scotia-a highly industrious area, trying to expand and to cooperate-should be commended. Hats off to them. This is one of Canada's worthy projects and I hope it will be carried through.

wish the minister would relax. I am afraid I might raise his blood pressure a few points. This bothers me no end. Another question I would like to ask the minister is what consideration is being given to the opening of a new mine on the north side of Sydney harbour? I am sure the minister is very familiar with all this. The Princess colliery is operating on the north side and two or three other mines on the south side of Sydney harbour. They are all scheduled for closing by 1973 under the plan put forward by Devco. Mr. Blackmore said in committee that production per man had gone up tremendously. In view of this I asked him 
whether he would not consider maintaining the Princess colliery in operation. He could not say very much at that point, but he did say that we would have to wait and see what develops because what might be a good situation today might be a bad one tomorrow. Could the minister advise whether any consideration has been given to opening a new mine? The miners now have to go out more than three miles under the Atlantic ocean to get the coal and the long hauls involved in bringing the coal to the surface naturally increase the cost of production. While the phasing out of the Princess mine was taking place it would be possible to prepare new slopes on the other seams. By opening a new seam, naturally you are going to get cheaper coal because it is not going to cost as much to bring the coal to the surface. I was hoping the minister could take that into consideration in his discussions with Devco, since I am sure he works with them quite closely.
I should like to reply to some of the points that were made by the cabinet representative from Nova Scotia. He stated that the $25 million to which reference was made some years ago was never promised. I must advise him, and I am sorry he is not here at the moment, that this promise was used in Liberal advertising prior to the election of 1965. With regard to his remarks concerning the points brought up by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, I may say we are all in favour of expanding the economy of Cape Breton Island. We are very pleased that the provincial and federal governments have gone into the oil business on the strait of Canso. We are very happy about any progress that is made in maintaining industries or bringing new industries into any part of Cape Breton Island. I think that what was worrying the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, and what worries me, is the fact that this development is 90 miles away. In the Glace Bay area and the Sydney Mines area mines are being closed down. What is going to take their place? We have people there almost of working age and there will be a number of people displaced. I would think it would only be right and proper to establish some industries close to the particular areas affected. This is the crux of the question at the moment. Is Devco going to give consideration to promoting industries in these areas?
Before I leave the cabinet minister from Nova Scotia, I may say I was glad to see him here today because I have been a bit worried about that hon. gentleman. He has no part to play in this house any more. He used to be

What I was suggesting, Mr. Chairman, was that this should be part of Devco's objectives.
With reference to my comment about the lack of concrete proposals in the plan that was presented to the committee, the minister said that the time had been too brief for this, that the issues are very complex and that we could not expect much more. I enjoyed the minister's comment about the relative efficiency of privately-owned versus publicly-owned enterprises. My point was not necessarily that it can be inferred that publicly owned enterprises are more efficient; I simply asked the non-rhetorical question whether the minister had any information which would lead the committee to draw some conclusions in this respect. Obviously, as a result of what information he did have in this regard the question still remains very much an open one, at least to me.
I was interested to note that the minister referred to the high level of morale which perhaps had contributed to the efficiency of the enterprise. This may be an indication that the sense of involvement and immediate concern evidenced by those who work for an enterprise has a direct relationship to its efficiency and may point to the necessity for some kind of legislation in this area to involve those who work in our enterprises at a higher level of intensity.
May I conclude with one general observation with reference to the minister's rather ringing defence of what is being done by Devco. I share the minister's belief that what Devco is doing compared with what has been done in public enterprises elsewhere in the country, and certainly in private enterprises, 
represents a very significant improvement. But I do not think he should suggest that it is up to the members of the opposition to stand and laud the government for what is being done; I do not think that is our function. The situation is an improvenent as a result of which most of the workers have benefited to a substantial degree.
I am a member of the opposition, and although the minister is not personally responsible he is a member of the cabinet that must be held responsible for what the government has done in the last few years for the average person in this country. Here one cannot make the same kind of defence. There is no capital gains tax. The Freedman report, which was published three years ago, still remains to be implemented. The government has failed to do a whole range of things that could be done for our workers, not only in the province of Nova Scotia but all across Canada. Certainly the government cannot take any pride for things done on this score.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
speechtext:
Devco is authorized by the law to promote industrial development on Cape Breton Island. The only restriction is that the development be industrial. Devco is not a substitute, of course, for the department. The department has its own duties. When the minister says that there have been negotiations with unions I think it will be found that he erred.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not understand in what I am wrong. Is it because I used the word "unions"?

I think the minister referred to negotiations or discussions with the unions involved. This is not the case. I think it will be established by reading the reports of the area development committee that this was not a negotiated plan. According to the information presented to the committee, this plan was drawn up and presented for approval.
The minister spoke of how well Cape Bretoners are treated, implying that we ought to be most grateful for the grant which the federal government pays toward maintenance of coal operations. I think reference was made to a subsidy having been paid over a period of 40 years. By the same token, would it not be interesting to look at the protection afforded the uranium industry in which the Prime Minister is personally involved, since part of that industry has dealings with his constituency?
Cheap.

At the same time let us look at that colossal white elephant which will require subsidies, subventions or what have you from now until eternity. I speak of the St. Lawrence seaway which was to benefit the area between Montreal and Toronto.
Shame.

Did anyone ever say clearly what the cost would be to support this white elephant? We hear talk about subventions on coal over the years. What was invested in the seaway? More than $500 million, and it will be a burden on the Canadian taxpayer forever. If they want to begin cutting out these things which they claim they are supporting, why not cut out the seaway?
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I see some hon. members are laughing. I invite them to check into this. They will be able to verify my statement that the seaway was built for the purpose of providing hydro for the sake of Ontario and Quebec. It was supposed to bring the farmers six cents more on every bushel of grain sold. But the farmers have the same problem today as they did then. It has been before the house day after
December 9, 1968

day for the last three weeks. They are still looking for box cars to carry their grain.
The minister implies that Cape Breton should be grateful for what is being done for the island. I suggest members should look around at what is being spent in support of other industries in this country and keep in mind that on the very day the corporation came before the committee saying that one of its biggest problems was transportation, an announcement came from the west coast that Kaiser was thinking about shipping coal from Cardiff, Wales. And the development corporation complains about a transportation problem!
Certainly we have a transportation problem, but it is mostly underground. Dr. Donald never went down to see it, though. The government put so much faith in his report they were willing to condemn the report of a previous commissioner who maintained there were 190 million tons of Cape Breton coal which could still be economically mined. Dr. Donald never went to the Cape Breton coalfields. He never went into a mine. But the previous commissioner did, and if the minister would read his report, which is available to him, he will see it is estimated there that 190 million tons of Cape Breton coal could still be economically brought to the surface.
The minister referred to the preamble to the bill. I would ask him to look at it closely and show me where there is authority given to the corporation to phase out this coal mining operation over a five year period in accordance with the plan to which reference has been made. I will read the preamble:
Whereas it has been estimated that the realistic working life of the Sydney coalfield on the Island of Cape Breton is only about 15 years and that as a result of rising operating costs the future operation of the mines in the coalfield will require the continuance on an increasing scale of the subsidies and other government assistance which have been provided over a period of almost 40 years-
They are rubbing it in. For 40 years the government has been helping them, it says.
And whereas the mines in the Sydney coalfield are faced with imminent closure unless a substantial capital investment is made for their rehabilitation and modernization and as a result of the aforementioned factors and the substantial dependence of the people of Sydney and the surrounding area and of the economy of the Island of Cape Breton on the coal mining operations in the coalfield, a critical situation exists on the island which is a concern to Canada as a whole;
And whereas it is considered desirable and the governments of Canada and Nova Scotia have agreed that a Crown corporation be established
Supply-Regional Development to promote and assist the financing and development of industry on the island to provide employment outside the coal producing industry and broaden the base of the economy of the island, and to acquire the interests of the major coal producer in the Sydney coalfield and reorganize and operate the mines with a view to the rationalization of coal production therefrom and the progressive withdrawal of the corporation from such production in accordance with a plan that takes into account progress in providing employment outside the coal producing industry and in broadening the base of the island's economy;
Where in that preamble does the corporation get the idea, as expressed on October 1,. 1968, that it can close down this mining operation? It is stated here in the second paragraph of the report: "It is the intention of the corporation to reduce coal mining employment as quickly as possible." Let the minister show me how the corporation has been guided by the preamble to this bill, or, for that matter, by any portion of this legislation.
The minister should become acquainted with the terms of this measure. I would refer him to what appears a little farther on in section 19 where it is stated:
(b) in accordance with approved budgets, paid to the corporation from time to time as required by it amounts not exceeding in the aggregate twenty-five million dollars for the purposes of reorganizing and rehabilitating the coal mining and related works and undertakings referred to in section 15 and for preparatory work in connection with conduct by the corporation of coal mining and related operations.
If the minister would read what section 15-says he would find it does not detract from the argument I am making now. The people of Cape Breton have been waiting for the fulfillment of promises made to them by this and previous governments with respect to the coal operation. They do not consider that the present and previous governments have taken into account the manner in which the nation was served by Cape Breton miners during the war when coal was so urgently needed. The corporation said it would spend $25 million on reorganizing the industry and rehabilitating the men concerned. Now it comes out with a report promising: We shall rid you of these men in five years.
The hon. gentleman talks about his concern for the unions. He says he believes there should be discussion with the unions. At the same time, the man in charge of the coal division of the corporation says before the committee that there is nothing in the legislation which requires the corporation to negotiate. According to him, these matters had not been discussed with the unions involved, and we were "drawing a thin line".

December 9, 1968
